2026-11-22.title: Fourth Sunday of the Dedication of the Church · Feast of Christ the King
2026-11-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (Syro-Malabar Liturgical Calendar)

Israel rejects the Lord as King
King of kings and Lord of lords
2026-11-22.alt: Last Sunday of the liturgical year. Next Sunday (29 November) the new liturgical year begins with the First Sunday of Annunciation (Suvara), First Set.
2026-11-22.verse: Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.”
theo: The liturgical year ends with a crown. On the last Sunday of Qudash Edtha the Church proclaims Christ the King. Pope Pius XI instituted the feast in 1925 (Quas Primas) for a world that was trying to organise itself without God; the question is no less urgent today.

The readings show two kinds of kingship. Melchizedek, “king of Salem” (peace) and “priest of God Most High”, brings out bread and wine and blesses Abraham: a mysterious figure of Christ, King and Priest, who offers bread and wine. Centuries later Israel demands “a king like other nations”, and God tells Samuel: “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.” Every time we choose earthly powers over God, we repeat Israel's demand.

Before Pilate, bound and condemned, Jesus says: “My kingdom is not from this world.” His kingship does not come from armies, money or votes; it comes from the truth. “For this I was born… to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.” His throne is the Cross; his crown is of thorns.

Revelation shows the end: heaven opened, a rider called Faithful and True, his robe dipped in blood, his name “The Word of God”, and on his robe: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” The Church, the Bride, ends her year by bowing before her King and Bridegroom. The question for each of us: does Christ reign in my home, my work, my phone, my choices?
conn: Melchizedek's bread and wine (Genesis 14:18) and Psalm 110:4, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” are applied to Christ in Hebrews 7. The Fathers saw in this offering a figure of the Eucharist.
Israel's demand (1 Samuel 8:5) echoes in the crowd's cry before Pilate: “We have no king but the emperor” (John 19:15). Both reject God's kingship.
Daniel 7:13–14 sees “one like a son of man” receiving an everlasting kingdom. Jesus applies this to himself before the high priest (Mark 14:62).
Pilate wrote “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (John 19:19–20): the first public proclamation of Christ's kingship, in the languages of the world.
altar: Melchizedek, king and priest, offered bread and wine; Christ, our King and High Priest, offers himself under the signs of bread and wine. At the Qurbana the King comes not to be served but to serve, and to give his life. To receive him is to accept his reign in us.
outline: Ask: who really rules your life? Look at your calendar, your bank statement and your phone's screen time.
Melchizedek's bread and wine point to Christ, King of peace and eternal Priest.
Point 2 · “We want a king like the nations”
Israel rejected God as King. We do the same when money, power or opinion rule us.
Point 3 · A kingdom not of this world
Christ reigns from the Cross, by truth and love. Whoever belongs to the truth listens to his voice.
The rider of Revelation: King of kings and Lord of lords. The year ends at his feet.
live: Place a picture or crucifix of Christ the King prominently and consecrate your family to him.
Choose truth in one situation where a lie would be easier.
Name one thing that rules you instead of God, and dethrone it this week.
fathers: On John 18: “Hear, Jews and Gentiles… I do not hinder your rule in this world. My kingdom is not of this world. Come and believe; do not be afraid” (Tractates on John 115).
He sees Melchizedek's offering of bread and wine as a figure of the Lord's sacrifice (Letter 63).
magis: Christ reigns in minds, wills and hearts; peace is possible only in the Kingdom of Christ.
The duty of offering God genuine worship concerns man both individually and socially; the Church announces Christ's kingship over all creation.
saints: 24 November: Vietnamese martyrs (Latin calendar). 28 November (celebrated for 29 November): St Andrew the Apostle.
2026-11-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, Priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, reign in our hearts, our families and our society. Make us belong to the truth and listen to your voice, until we see you in your glory. Amen.

illus: In 1927 the Mexican Jesuit Blessed Miguel Pro was shot by a firing squad during the persecution of the Church. He stretched out his arms like a cross and cried, “¡Viva Cristo Rey!” (Long live Christ the King!). Earthly rulers took his life; they could not take his King.

family.explain: Jesus told Pilate he is a King, but his kingdom is not like earthly kingdoms. He rules with love and truth. We want him to be King of our family.
family.intention: We pray that Jesus may reign in our home and in our country.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we show that Jesus is the King of our family?”

catechism: Christ reigns; he will come again to judge.
kidsaint: A cheerful Mexican priest who served people secretly in disguise when the Church was persecuted. Before he died he cried, “Long live Christ the King!” Lesson: be brave and joyful for Jesus.
term: King of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham with bread and wine (Genesis 14). The Letter to the Hebrews sees in him a figure of Christ, the eternal Priest-King.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the liturgical year ends today with a crown. We proclaim Christ the King. Next Sunday a new year begins with the announcement of his coming; today we kneel before him as Lord of all.

In the first reading a mysterious king appears: Melchizedek, king of Salem, which means peace, and priest of God Most High. He brings bread and wine and blesses Abraham. The Fathers of the Church saw in him a figure of Christ, King of peace and eternal Priest, who offers bread and wine that become his Body and Blood.

Then we hear a sad story. Israel tells Samuel: “Give us a king like other nations.” God says: “They have not rejected you; they have rejected me as their king.” Brothers and sisters, how often do we do the same? We let money be king, or power, or what people say, or our phone. Christ is not removed from his throne by atheists only; he is pushed aside quietly by Christians who let other things rule.

Before Pilate Jesus stands bound. Pilate asks, “Are you a king?” Jesus answers: “My kingdom is not from this world… I came to testify to the truth.” His throne is the Cross; his crown is of thorns; his power is love. And Revelation shows him at the end: King of kings and Lord of lords.
So today, at the end of the year, let us ask honestly: does Christ reign in my home? in my business? in my words? in my screen? Let us give him the crown today. Jesus, reign in me. Amen.
kids: Children, what does a king wear? A crown! And what does he sit on? A throne!
Jesus is a King too, the greatest King of all! But his crown was made of thorns and his throne was the Cross, because he loved us so much.
Let's make Jesus the King of our hearts. Say together: “Jesus, you are my King!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, on this last Sunday of the liturgical year we proclaim Christ as King of the universe. We sing, we crown His image, we carry Him in procession. But let us remember what kind of crown He wore on earth: a crown of thorns.

When Pilate asked Jesus whether He was a king, Jesus answered: my kingdom is not from this world. He came to testify to the truth, and everyone who belongs to the truth listens to His voice (John 18:36–37). Pilate had soldiers, a palace and the power of Rome. Jesus had nothing but truth and love. Yet two thousand years later Pilate is remembered only because his name is in our Creed, and Jesus reigns in the hearts of millions.

Above the Cross the soldiers nailed an inscription: this is the King of the Jews (Luke 23:38). They meant it as a mockery, but it was the truth. Christ reigns from the Cross. His power is not to take life but to give it. And the first one to recognise His kingship was a dying criminal who said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Jesus answered: today you will be with me in Paradise (Luke 23:42–43).

So the real question today is not whether Christ is King of the universe. He is, whether the world accepts it or not. The question is whether He is King of my heart. Does He reign over my tongue, my money, my phone, my family, my work, my politics? Or have I kept some area of my life closed to Him, a little kingdom of my own?

As we end this liturgical year, let us open every door to Christ. Let us serve as He served, especially the least of His brothers and sisters. And when we receive Him in this Holy Qurbana, let us say with the good thief: Jesus, remember me in your kingdom. That prayer is enough to save a whole life.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the Kingship of Christ in the Church's teaching
intro: Pope Pius XI established this feast in 1925 (Quas Primas), when nations were turning away from God. Its message is even more urgent today.

sub: By nature: He is the Son of God (Colossians 1:15–17).
By conquest: He redeemed us by His blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, this feast is younger than many of us think. Pope Pius XI established it in 1925, in the encyclical Quas Primas. Europe had just come out of a terrible war, ideologies were rising that put the State or the race in the place of God, and many nations were living as if God did not exist. The Pope proclaimed: Christ is King, of individuals, of families and of societies.

Why is Christ King? First, by His very nature: He is the eternal Son of God, through whom and for whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15–17). Second, by conquest: He redeemed us, not with silver or gold, but with His precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19). Third, because the Father has given Him all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). Daniel saw one like a son of man receiving an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14).

His Kingdom is already present and not yet complete. The Second Vatican Council says that the Church is the Kingdom of Christ already present in mystery (Lumen Gentium 3). It grows quietly like a mustard seed. But it will be fulfilled only when Christ comes again in glory, when He hands over the Kingdom to the Father and God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; CCC 671). Until then we pray every day: Thy kingdom come.

Does this feast have anything to say to society? Yes. The Catechism teaches that Christians have the duty to bring the spirit of the Gospel into the life of society, its customs, laws and structures (CCC 2105). That means defending the dignity of every human life from conception to natural death, working for justice and peace, caring for the poor and the migrant. It does not mean forcing faith on anyone; the Church respects freedom of conscience. We propose Christ by our witness.

Through Baptism we share in Christ's royal office, which means to serve (CCC 786). The King washed feet. So let us end this liturgical year by renewing our allegiance to Christ, and let us show it by serving the least of His brothers and sisters. Then His Kingdom will come, a little more, in our homes and in our land.

intro: On the last Sunday of the year the Church proclaims Christ the King: Priest-King prefigured by Melchizedek, rejected by Israel's demand for an earthly king, crowned with thorns before Pilate, and revealed as King of kings.

sub: Melchizedek, king of Salem, offers bread and wine and blesses Abraham.
Christ is the eternal Priest-King.
At the Qurbana the King gives himself to us.
q: And King Melchizedek of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High. He blessed him and said, “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth.”
He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is called The Word of God.
points.apply: Receive Communion this Sunday as an act of homage to your King.

sub: Israel demands a king “like other nations”.
God says: they have rejected me.
We do the same when money, power or opinion rule us.
q: And the LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.”

Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my followers would be fighting to keep me from being handed over to the Jews. But as it is, my kingdom is not from here.”
points.apply: Name one thing that rules you instead of God, and dethrone it.

sub: Daniel sees the Son of Man receive an everlasting kingdom.
Christ reigns by truth: whoever belongs to the truth hears his voice.
At the end every knee will bow.
q: To him was given dominion and glory and kingship, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away.
On his robe and on his thigh he has a name inscribed, “King of kings and Lord of lords.”
points.apply: Consecrate your family to Christ the King this week.

concl: The year ends at the feet of the King.
Let him reign in our homes, our work and our hearts.
